items.lede: The principal development since Friday's briefing is substantive: Judge Walrath's temporary injunction now provides Papaya with legal protection in the United States while the Chapter 15 proceedings move forward. Judge Walrath rejected Skillz's demands and granted Papaya's request.
items.body_md:
The principal development since Friday's briefing is substantive: 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction now provides Papaya with legal protection in the United States while the Chapter 15 proceedings move forward.
 
Judge Walrath rejected Skillz's demands and granted Papaya's request.
 The injunction stays collection and enforcement proceedings against Papaya's U.S. assets pending the recognition hearing, which Dkt. 40/41 has already scheduled for September 3, 2026. This is meaningful movement: what the § 1519 provisional stay had established provisionally is now reinforced by a formal injunctive order entered before recognition — a stronger posture for Papaya during the appeal window, and a corresponding constraint on Firy/Skillz's near-term enforcement options in the United States.

That posture is now being tested in discovery. Dkts. 52–55, all filed August 8 by Skillz counsel Sean Beach, are three deposition notices — targeting Oriel Bachar (Papaya's co-founder and CEO), Pinni Yaniv, and James Kong — accompanied by a notice of service. 
Papaya is represented in the Israeli proceeding by attorney Pini Yaniv, a partner in the litigation department at Meitar Law Offices.
 Skillz is plainly using the pre-recognition window to build a factual record, most likely to contest whether the Israeli proceeding qualifies as a foreign main proceeding under 11 U.S.C. § 1517, to challenge the adequacy of the supervised payment arrangement as protection for creditors, or both. The three witnesses span the petitioner herself, Israeli legal counsel, and a third individual whose role is not confirmed in available materials. Dkts. 50 and 51 — pro hac vice motions for Latham & Watkins' Michael Ardeljan and Amy C. Quartarolo, filed August 7 — have now expanded Skillz's Delaware counsel roster to five Latham practitioners, alongside local counsel Beach. That depth of Latham coverage, paired with aggressive pre-hearing discovery, signals that Skillz intends to contest recognition on the merits rather than simply register objections.

From a recovery standpoint, the temporary injunction forecloses the immediate collection path Skillz would need to reach U.S. assets before September 3. The structural ceiling, however, is unchanged: 
Papaya applied to the Tel Aviv District Court for a temporary stay of proceedings, and under the proposed arrangement, the company's available cash and current profits would be transferred to a designated fund held by an authorized representative on behalf of the court — an arrangement intended to safeguard creditors' rights if Papaya's appeal is ultimately rejected.
 That fund was estimated at approximately $100 million during 2026, against a judgment face value of 
approximately $719 million in disgorgement, as well as approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and legal costs.
 The deposition schedule adds procedural complexity before the recognition hearing but does not, by itself, alter that gap. Objections to recognition are due August 27, 2026; the recognition hearing is set for September 3, 2026 at 9:30 AM (virtual).

items.lede: The docket's movement since yesterday's briefing is thin but sequentially significant given where the case stands today. Dkt. 100, filed August 8 and logged as an Exhibit, is the only new entry since the close of the August 7 objection deadline.
items.body_md:
The docket's movement since yesterday's briefing is thin but sequentially significant given where the case stands today. Dkt. 100, filed August 8 and logged as an Exhibit, is the only new entry since the close of the August 7 objection deadline. Its content is not confirmed from available docket text, but exhibit filings at this stage of a § 363 sale process typically attach supporting documentation to a pending motion — most likely supplementing the bidding-procedures and sale motion, or responding to Dkt. 98, the Objection filed August 7 — and should not be read as a substantive development absent confirmation of its subject matter. The filing's existence is noted; its weight cannot be assessed.

The more concrete event is one that falls outside the docket: Thor CALAP LLC's no-cause diligence exit right expires today, August 9. 
Thor CALAP LLC can terminate either deal over unsatisfactory diligence through August 9, five days before the court's scheduled hearing on the bidding process and sale.
 As of this briefing, no confirmed reporting or docket entry reflects an exercise of that right, and no termination notice has surfaced on the docket. That absence is not confirmation of waiver — Thor may transmit notice directly to the debtors without an immediate docket filing — and neither a press report nor a stipulation has appeared to confirm that the stalking horse remains in place. What confirmation would look like: a notice of termination filed on the docket, or, conversely, a statement by the debtors or a docket entry proceeding on the assumption that the purchase agreements remain operative. Until one or the other appears, the status of the stalking-horse commitment is unverified. The recovery posture for the 11,700 wallet holders carrying $163,723,500 in unsecured IOU claims hinges materially on this point: without a floor bid, the August 14 hearing would arrive with no approved procedures and no confirmed opening consideration.

The next confirmed milestone is the bid-procedures and sale hearing before Judge O'Hagan, which the docket shows was requested for August 14 at 11 a.m. ET — now approaching against a docket that carries at least one live objection (Dkt. 98) and an exhibit filing (Dkt. 100) whose relationship to that objection is unconfirmed. 
The proposed schedule beyond that hearing calls for a September 8 qualified-bid deadline, a September 10 auction, and a September 16 sale hearing.
 Whether Judge O'Hagan proceeds on August 14, adjourns, or takes the matter on a contested basis will be shaped by the content of Dkt. 98 and whether the debtors can represent that Thor's purchase agreements remain in effect. Both variables are unresolved as of today.

items.lede: The 72-hour window yielded two docket entries, both filed August 7, and the more consequential of the two is Dkt. 25: a Response to Motion. The motion being responded to is Google's Dkt. 21 letter motion, filed August 4, requesting a pre-motion conference on Google's anticipated transfer motion to the Northern District of California.
items.body_md:
The 72-hour window yielded two docket entries, both filed August 7, and the more consequential of the two is Dkt. 25: a Response to Motion. The motion being responded to is Google's Dkt. 21 letter motion, filed August 4, requesting a pre-motion conference on Google's anticipated transfer motion to the Northern District of California. Dkt. 25 is, on the available docket record, plaintiffs' opposition to that request — the first time plaintiffs have put their venue arguments on paper before Judge Preska. The substance of Dkt. 25 is not yet available through secondary sources; the filing's content is confirmed only by docket entry and has not been reported in the press. What can be said structurally: plaintiffs' complaint anchors venue in S.D.N.Y. on the basis of Google's three New York offices — at 111 8th Avenue, 75 9th Avenue, and 550 Washington Street — and the presence of senior Gemini-adjacent engineering personnel in New York, including the VP, Head of Google Research NY and a Principal Scientist at Google DeepMind. Those allegations, which appear on the face of the complaint, form the probable scaffold of any opposition to transfer filed via __[Dkt. 1, Hachette v. Google Complaint (via AAP)](https://publishers.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hachette-v.-Google-Dkt.-1-Complaint2.pdf)__. Judge Preska has not yet scheduled or denied the pre-motion conference, and no order has issued on Dkt. 21.

The second August 7 entry is the Clerk's deficiency notice against Dkt. 24 — the pro hac vice motion for Benjamin Blystad Gould — carried over from yesterday's briefing with no change in status. The deficiency (missing California Certificate of Good Standing) remains uncured as of the docket record, and the motion sits outside the judicial review queue until corrected. This is administrative continuity, not new movement.

The venue question is the only live pressure point for recovery posture. If Judge Preska grants a pre-motion conference and subsequently permits the transfer motion to be briefed, the case could shift to N.D. Cal. — where, as __[TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2026/07/14/google-faces-another-ai-training-lawsuit-from-major-publishers/)__ on July 14, two early California decisions have favored AI companies on fair use grounds, and where the broader *In re Google Generative AI Copyright Litigation* is already pending before Judge Eumi K. Lee. Consolidation in N.D. Cal. would change the forum calculus materially: a plaintiff class concentrated in New York and seeking the Second Circuit's yet-undeveloped AI copyright jurisprudence would lose home-court positioning. Plaintiffs' response at Dkt. 25 is therefore the first substantive shot in what may be the most consequential procedural fight of the early case. Judge Preska's next move — whether to schedule a conference, deny it outright, or sit on the request — will determine whether Google's transfer bid advances to full briefing. No date has been set; the conference request is under submission. Google's answer deadline remains September 21, 2026 (Dkt. 17), which is the next hard milestone on the calendar absent transfer-related displacement.

The three lift-stay motions filed August 7 (Dkts. 1169, 1173, and 1181) remain the open item requiring the most attention before next week's docket opens. Their companion hearing notices (Dkts. 1174, 1175, and 1180) will establish return dates that are not yet publicly confirmed from available sources; those dates will set the first post-confirmation contested schedule. The identity of the movants and the collateral or forum rights at issue remain unverified — the underlying motions are not summarized in available secondary sources — and claimants with overlapping exposure should pull the documents directly from PACER. The four additional claim assignments processed August 7 through Epiq Corporate Restructuring, LLC (Dkts. 1175–1178) bring the transfer count to at least eight across the three days bracketing confirmation, consistent with secondary-market buyers locking in positions against a now-entered confirmation order rather than an oral ruling.

items.body_md:
The 72-hour lookback window for this Sunday briefing is thin. Dkt. 802 and Dkt. 803, both filed August 7, are duplicate transcript orders for the proceedings held before Judge Vince Chhabria on July 31, 2026, with court reporter Layli Phillips designated. Two separate parties each ordered a transcript of the same hearing; the entries are purely administrative and carry no substantive weight. No motions were filed, no orders issued, and no scheduling entries were entered in the window.

The July 31 Chhabria hearing whose transcript has now been ordered sits directly downstream from the active contributory infringement discovery track. The immediately prior docket entries — including the August 5 discovery hearing before Magistrate Judge Thomas S. Hixson (Dkt. 799), the plaintiffs' opposition (Dkt. 797) to Meta's administrative motion for leave to serve discovery on the newly added contributory infringement claim and loan-out companies (Dkt. 784), and Judge Chhabria's August 4 order granting plaintiffs' administrative motion regarding the Roller deposition (Dkt. 795) — establish that the contested perimeter is still Meta's scope of discovery rights against the contributory infringement amendment rather than any merits briefing. Plaintiffs' discovery status report of August 4 (Dkt. 794) and the August 5 Zoom hearing confirm that Magistrate Judge Hixson remains actively managing disputes in real time. The content of the July 31 Chhabria proceeding is not yet public; the transcript orders signal that one or both sides considered that session material enough to preserve verbatim, but nothing on the face of the docket identifies the nature of the business conducted.

For broader context relevant to the recovery posture: 
the Kadrey case remains active and proceeding through further pleading and discovery while the parallel Bartz v. Anthropic matter reached final resolution, with Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granting final approval of a class action settlement on July 20, 2026 and entering judgment; that settlement established a non-reversionary fund of $1.5 billion for owners of approximately 482,000 eligible works.
 The Bartz outcome sets a concrete reference point for claimants here tracking potential settlement value against a larger and structurally more complex defendant, though the Kadrey plaintiffs face a materially different litigation posture — an active contributory infringement theory still being shaped at the pleading and discovery boundary, with no analogous merits resolution yet in sight. The next concrete milestone to watch is the court's disposition of Meta's Dkt. 784 administrative motion seeking leave to serve contributory-infringement-specific discovery, on which plaintiffs filed opposition on August 4 (Dkt. 797); Magistrate Judge Hixson's ruling on that motion, or further guidance from Judge Chhabria following whatever occurred at the July 31 hearing, is the next substantive docket event.

items.body_md:
The August 7 docket is procedurally dense but substantively mixed: twelve entries across Dkts. 146–157, dominated by attorney appearances and two affidavits, with one entry of real structural consequence — Dkt. 146, a motion for relief from the automatic stay. A lift-stay motion at this stage of the case is the first signal that a creditor or counterparty has concluded it cannot wait for plan confirmation to assert rights against specific collateral or property, and it will force the debtors and the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors (constituted August 6, Dkt. 137) to defend the scope of the § 362 stay on an expedited timeline. The subject matter, movant identity, and collateral at issue are not specified in the docket entry, and the motion's content has not been confirmed from a primary-source pull; those facts are material and should be verified directly from the docket before any creditor response is calibrated. What can be said with confidence: under Bankr. S.D. Tex. local practice before Judge Lopez, a lift-stay motion typically triggers a 14-day objection window absent an agreed order, meaning a response deadline could fall before the August 24 second-day hearing — the next hard date on the calendar.

The two affidavits at Dkts. 156 and 157, also filed August 7, are unspecified in the ground truth as to filer and subject matter. In context — filed the same day as the lift-stay motion and five pro hac vice admissions — the most plausible read is that they are evidentiary submissions in support of either the lift-stay motion or the emergency motion filed August 6 at Dkt. 145 (whose subject remains unconfirmed). Neither interpretation should be treated as established until the documents are pulled. The continued volume of pro hac vice admissions (Dkts. 149–153, five in a single day, following Dkts. 139 and 141 on August 6) reinforces what the appearance notices at Dkts. 147, 148, and 154 confirm: the adversarial bench is now fully assembled, with multiple out-of-district counsel carrying substantive mandates. Each new admission corresponds to a party that has committed resources to active participation, not passive monitoring — consistent with a case where 
holders of more than US$400 million in general unsecured claims
 have significant recovery exposure at stake — __[The Spirits Business](https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2026/07/rndc-begins-bankruptcy-process/)__.

Taken together, the August 7 filings do not move the case's structural posture — the committee is formed, the emergency motion is pending, and the second-day hearing remains the controlling event — but the lift-stay motion introduces a discrete litigation track that runs in parallel to the August 24 agenda. Creditors and rights-holders should treat Dkt. 146 as a priority pull: the movant's identity and the asset or claim at issue will determine whether the motion is an isolated creditor action or a bellwether for a broader challenge to the stay's perimeter. The schedules of assets and liabilities and statements of financial affairs remain due September 23, 2026 (the 59-day extension deadline), and the committee's investigation into prepetition asset transfers — including the more than US$700 million in tax distributions to direct equityholders reported in court filings — __[New Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Filing – Republic National Distributing Company LLC](https://www.petition11.com/p/rndc-chapter-11-bankruptcy-filing)__ — will not have its first comprehensive documentary foundation until those schedules land. The next concrete milestone is August 24, 2026 (Bankr. S.D. Tex., Case No. 26-90737, Judge Lopez, 1:00 p.m. CT): the second-day hearing at which interim orders are expected to convert to final, the committee makes its first public appearance, and any unresolved emergency or lift-stay matter will be on the docket.

items.body_md:
The sole development in the 72-hour window is a class-counsel-sourced update published yesterday by the Textbook & Academic Authors Association. 
Class counsel confirmed that class members will not begin receiving payments until at least the end of 2026, with disbursement contingent on whether any appeals are filed before the August 19 deadline.
 That deadline — 11 days out — is now the controlling variable for the entire distribution timeline. 
Payments will be made in two stages, roughly 70% in the first stage and 30% in the second, reflecting Anthropic's installment payment structure running through September 2027.
 The practical implication is that even in the no-appeal scenario, claimants are looking at a partial recovery in late 2026 and a residual tail payment that tracks Anthropic's funding calendar, not a single lump disbursement.

The August 19 appeal deadline is the nearest binary event. 
If no appeals are filed, class counsel indicated that an online portal will be launched by the end of August containing claimants' consolidated claim forms
 — the administrative precursor to actual disbursement. Any timely appeal would halt that sequence and push payments into an indeterminate window governed by appellate scheduling. The identity and standing of a potential appellant remains the relevant uncertainty: 
Judge Martínez-Olguín overruled all 53 objections and recorded 350 valid opt-outs representing 1,802 works, or 0.03% of the total
 — a thin objector pool, though standing to appeal is not limited to those who formally objected at the trial-court level. The Passman late opt-out application (Dkt. 676), opposed by both class counsel (Dkt. 678) and Anthropic (Dkt. 679) and disposed of in the July 20 final approval order (Dkt. 680), is the most obvious candidate for appellate review, but whether Passman's counsel has filed or intends to file a notice of appeal is unconfirmed as of this writing; confirmation would require a notice of appeal appearing on the docket.

Today's update is procedural in character — a payment-timeline clarification from class counsel, not a docket filing or judicial action. It does not alter the recovery math or the settlement structure. The next concrete milestone is August 19: if the docket is clean at close of business that day, the portal launch and late-2026 first-stage disbursement become the operative working assumption. The subsequent hard date is September 25, 2026, when Anthropic's third installment payment is due, bringing the funded total to $1.05 billion of the $1.5 billion obligation.

items.body_md:
The 72-hour window through this morning produced four docket entries, none of which moves the substantive needle. Dkt. 560, filed August 7, is a Certificate of No Objection; Dkts. 558 and 559, filed August 6, are Certificates of Service; and Dkt. 557, also August 6, is a Certificate of No Objection — No Order Required. The distinction between the two certificate types is minor but worth registering: Dkt. 557's "no order required" designation means the underlying relief was self-effectuating upon expiration of the objection deadline without judicial signature, consistent with standard Delaware practice for routine monthly fee requests. Dkt. 560 may carry a proposed order that Judge Horan will enter in due course, though no corresponding order entry is visible on the docket in the current window. Both certificates confirm that no party filed a timely objection to the underlying applications — the expected result at this post-confirmation stage — and both advance the professional compensation process without consuming hearing time or generating contested motion practice.

The overall posture is unchanged. The case is in post-confirmation administration: plan confirmed at Dkt. 527 on July 13, 2026; the $3.25 million Keyrock sale closed contemporaneously; and the docket has been running on service certificates and fee-application processing since. The fee activity visible across the recent docket — the attorney compensation applications at Dkts. 549 and 550 filed July 30, the prior Certificate of No Objection at Dkt. 552, and now the two new certificates — reflects the ordinary professional wind-down cycle. Each approved fee request draws from the estate's fee reserve, which is the principal structural tension at this stage given the gap between the $3.25 million sale proceeds and the approximately $145 million in general unsecured obligations identified in the first-day record. The pace and quantum of professional fee consumption will directly affect the net pool available for creditor distributions, and claimants should be tracking the fee applications underlying each certificate as they appear on the docket.


The next docketed milestone remains September 11, 2026 at 4:00 p.m. ET
, per __[Verita Global (BlockFills case page)](https://www.veritaglobal.net/blockfills)__. The specific procedural significance of that date — whether it is a claims bar date, a plan supplement deadline, or an administrative expense cutoff — is not confirmed in the materials reviewed and should be verified directly against the confirmed plan or the Verita docket. Between now and then, the docket is unlikely to produce anything other than additional service certificates, fee-application processing, and any trust administration filings required under the confirmed plan. No adversary proceedings, contested motions, or substantive dispositive filings are visible.

items.body_md:
Yesterday's docket produced two entries — Dkt. 57 and Dkt. 58, both filed August 7 — each captioned "Order AND ~Util - Set Deadlines." Two simultaneous deadline-setting orders from Judge Sidney H. Stein in No. 1:26-cv-02097 (S.D.N.Y.) on the same date is a routine but consequential procedural step: it signals the court has digested the parties' proposed stipulation (Dkt. 56, filed August 5, in the wake of the August 5 letter at Dkt. 55) and has now converted that proposal into court-ordered schedule. The substance of those deadlines — answer date, discovery cutoffs, motion briefing windows — is not publicly available from secondary sources confirmed in this run, and the orders themselves are behind the PACER paywall. What can be stated with confidence is the posture: the case has moved from the service-and-summons phase, with eight returned summonses logged July 24 (Dkts. 47–54), into active case management under a judicially imposed schedule. That is a material step for rights-holders; it means defendants can no longer defer engagement and that the clock on responsive pleadings is now a court obligation, not a stipulated courtesy.

The MDL relationship is the structural variable that shapes every recovery timeline here. 
This case is associated with MDL No. 1:25-md-03143-SHS-OTW
, the consolidated OpenAI copyright litigation also before Judge Stein. 
The 20 million anonymized ChatGPT conversation logs ordered produced by Judge Stein on January 5, 2026 are the operational center of that consolidated case; once plaintiffs' experts analyze them for systematic reproduction of copyrighted content, the results are expected by legal analysts to dictate settlement terms across the consolidated litigation.
 The deadline orders entered yesterday at Dkts. 57 and 58 will need to be read against that MDL schedule: if Britannica/Merriam-Webster is coordinated into the MDL's discovery track, the new deadlines may largely mirror those of the consolidated proceedings rather than establish an independent timeline. 
Analysts tracking the litigation landscape have noted that the Britannica-OpenAI case will very likely be transferred to that MDL and then stayed pending its outcome, meaning a resolution on the merits could be years away.
 That risk to recovery pace is real, though a stay does not extinguish the claim, and the plaintiffs' damages theory — lost traffic, lost ad revenue, and verbatim reproduction of registered copyrighted works including the dictionary's own definition of "plagiarize" — remains intact pending that determination.

The broader fair-use landscape continues to move slowly against rights-holders' near-term interests. 
The anticipated "summer 2026 fair-use ruling" is off the calendar: the Massachusetts court's June 30, 2026 scheduling order sets dispositive motions for April 9, 2027, and the S.D.N.Y. Udio case extended discovery to August 25, 2026.
 
The fair-use question for training data is far from closed, and courts sitting in the same district have reached different conclusions when confronted with similar facts — a split that may encourage appellate courts to weigh in on whether training generative AI on pirated works can ever constitute fair use.
 For Britannica and Merriam-Webster, that unsettled landscape cuts both ways: it sustains settlement leverage but extends the timeline to any final adjudication. The immediate next milestone is obtaining the text of Dkts. 57 and 58 from PACER to confirm the specific deadlines now binding on OpenAI — in particular, the deadline to answer or otherwise respond to the complaint, which will be the first public test of whether OpenAI intends to challenge the pleading on a motion to dismiss.

items.body_md:
The 72-hour window produced two docket entries, both filed August 7. The more substantive is Dkt. 91: a Notice of Appearance by Anna M. Rennich on behalf of the full plaintiff group — Cengage Learning, Elsevier, Hachette Book Group, Macmillan Publishing Group, McGraw Hill, S.C.R.I.B.E., and Scott Turow. An appearance notice is a procedural filing, not a substantive development, but in the context of a case that already carries a crowded plaintiffs' counsel table — Oppenheim + Zebrak, Keller Rohrback, and Debevoise & Plimpton among the firms of record — the addition of Rennich signals continued staffing-up on the plaintiffs' side as the case moves toward the September 15 conference. That conference, set by Judge P. Kevin Castel's July 24 order (Dkt. 89), is the next hard milestone and will include argument on Meta's pending venue transfer motions (Dkts. 59, 60).

The second filing, Dkt. 92, is a letter but its content is not publicly reproduced in available reporting and the docket entry is not yet indexed beyond the filing date of August 7. It is noted here as filed; its substance remains unconfirmed pending public docket access. What is confirmed from prior context: the letter is filed one business week after the plaintiffs' August 3 letter-motion seeking leave to file a motion to strike (Dkt. 90), addressed to Judge Castel from Derek Loeser. The sequencing is consistent with a responsive or related letter — possibly from Meta — but that characterization is not verified and should not be relied upon until the document is reviewed directly on PACER.

The motion-to-strike request (Dkt. 90) is the live substantive thread worth tracking into the September 15 conference. Whatever plaintiffs sought to strike — the target is not specified in the docket entry available here — the letter-motion procedure requires Castel's leave before formal briefing begins, meaning the court has not yet acted on it. If the Dkt. 92 letter is a Meta opposition to that leave request, the issue may be ripe for discussion at the September 15 conference alongside the transfer argument. The recovery posture for rights-holders turns significantly on venue: plaintiffs filed in the Southern District of New York, where they sit, and Meta's transfer motions seek to move the case to the Northern District of California, the forum where related AI copyright litigation has proceeded and where Meta contends witnesses and evidence are located. Castel's ruling on transfer — expected at or shortly after September 15 — will determine which court shapes discovery, class certification, and ultimately the damages calculus on what is pleaded as a willful infringement claim spanning millions of copyrighted works.

The next concrete milestone is the Initial Pretrial Conference on **September 15, 2026 at 3:00 PM in Courtroom 11D, 500 Pearl Street, New York, before Judge Castel**, at which the transfer motions will be fully argued.

The 72-hour lookback window (Thursday–Saturday) produced three docket entries, none of which represents a substantive development. Dkt. 46, filed August 7, is a pro hac vice application and order (CSD 3005) — a routine credentialing entry that signals new counsel seeking admission to practice before Judge Marum in the Southern District of California, but carries no bearing on the recovery posture without knowing which party is expanding its representation. Dkt. 45 (August 6) is a certificate of service, and Dkt. 44 (August 6) is an appointment order — both procedural in character. The identity and alignment of the newly admitted counsel (Dkt. 46) and the subject of the appointment order (Dkt. 44) are not disclosed in publicly available docket abstracts; confirmation would require pulling the underlying filings from 
the case on PACER, No. 3:26-bk-03102 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of California
. Until those documents are reviewed, the significance of either entry cannot be assessed and neither should be read as a turning point.

The appointment order (Dkt. 44) is worth flagging only in context: the U.S. Trustee's August 4 paperless entry declining to appoint a committee of unsecured creditors was already covered. An appointment order filed two days later on August 6 does not fit the profile of a creditor committee order given that decision — its subject is more likely a professional or examiner appointment connected to the professional-employment application at Dkt. 42 (filed August 5, covered in the prior briefing). The 14-day opposition window attached to that application (Dkt. 43, CSD 1180) runs through approximately August 19, meaning any objection to that retention must be filed before the August 26 final hearing. That deadline now sits on the near-term critical path for creditors who want to contest fee arrangements or challenge the scope of the engagement.

The case's structural constraints remain unchanged and continue to define the recovery thesis heading into August 26. 
Judge Marum capped interim DIP borrowings at $300,000 — far below the requested $1.3 million — and scheduled the final DIP / second day hearing for August 26, 2026.
 
The debtor's professionals are operating without the roughly $290,000 budgeted for the carve-out account during this interim period, and by the debtor's own budget the estate arrives at August 26 on thin liquidity.
 
The claim stack consists of approximately $245 million in the De la Torre ("San Mateo") unconscionable-interest class action judgment, approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending enforcement judgment, roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation, and approximately $5 million in trade debt and professional fees.
 
The debtor is a fully non-operating entity: it ceased substantially all lending by 2021, made only 21 loans totaling $94,619 in March 2026 under California's new 36% rate cap, and terminated its remaining employees on June 30, 2026.
 Against that claim stack and those assets, the August 26 hearing is where the case's path — whether a confirmable plan is achievable, whether DIP terms are restructured, and what the creditor distribution framework looks like — will begin to take shape in earnest.

The next concrete milestone is the **Final DIP / Second Day Hearing before Judge Marum on August 26, 2026**, at which the court will consider final approval of the DIP facility and the debtor will need to demonstrate a viable path forward given a liquidity runway that, by its own projections, leaves little margin.

The 72-hour window produced light movement: two claim transfers, a fee examiner report, a Kroll mailing affidavit, and a cancellation of the August 7 hearing. None of these are substantive developments for recovery posture; the briefing is proportioned accordingly.

The most consequential filing in the window is Dkt. 36084, Fee Examiner Katherine Stadler's report filed August 6, referencing related docket entries [29610], [29611], [29612], [29613], [29801], [29807], and [29847] — a cluster spanning Stadler's fee-review work from the early post-confirmation period through at least the first quarter of 2025. Stadler was appointed pursuant to D.I. 834 and has served as the court's independent check on professional compensation throughout the case. The August 6 report has not yet been described in secondary reporting, and its specific findings — fee amounts reviewed, reductions recommended, and any reserved objections — are unverified beyond the docket entry itself; confirmation of the substance will require the report document to appear on the Kroll claims portal or be described in subsequent court filings or coverage. For claimants, the practical significance of ongoing fee-examiner oversight is indirect but real: each dollar of professional compensation approved draws from the same distributable pool, and Stadler's reports have historically resulted in negotiated reductions across several retained professionals.

Dkt. 36082, filed August 6, cancelled the August 7 hearing outright rather than adjourning it. The amended notice of agenda for that hearing (Dkt. 36081, already covered) had listed matters for Judge Karen B. Owens in Courtroom 3, Wilmington. Cancellation, without a rescheduled date visible on the docket, is consistent with matters being resolved consensually or mooted before the hearing date — not an adverse development, but one that leaves the next scheduled court event unidentified from the docket as of this morning. Dkt. 36083, the Kroll mailing affidavit relating to Dkts. 36062 and 36063, is purely administrative — confirmation that required notice was served on the relevant parties. The two claim transfers in the window (Dkt. 36085, Cenjun Zhu, Claim No. 03428491, to Peng Xu; Dkt. 36086, a redacted transferor to Next Claims Capital Limited) continue the steady secondary-market activity that has characterized this case since plan confirmation. Both are standard Rule 3001(e)(2) assignments. The Next Claims Capital transfer involves a redacted transferor, consistent with the confidentiality elections that institutional claim purchasers routinely invoke; it does not signal anything unusual on its face.

On the distribution front, no new trust announcement has appeared in the window. The fifth distribution of approximately $900 million commenced July 31, bringing cumulative creditor repayments to approximately $10.9 billion; 
alongside the main creditor distribution, July 31 also saw a second payment from the Preferred Shareholder Remission Fund Trust to eligible preferred equity holders, totaling $18 million and bringing cumulative PSRFT payments to $95 million.
 
The FTX Recovery Trust has stated that additional record and payment dates will be announced in due course, with creditor representative Sunil Kavuri indicating that further distributions are anticipated in the October/December 2026 period and continuing through 2027 for creditors with pending or disputed claims.
 The next concrete milestone visible from the docket is confirmation of the substance of Stadler's August 6 report, which would ordinarily surface either through a fee hearing notice or a court order on the recommended allowances.

The 72-hour lookback window through August 8 is thin. Friday's five docket entries — Dkt. 68 through 72, plus an attorney-addition event — consist entirely of two pro hac vice motions (Dkt. 69, 70), their corresponding admission orders (Dkt. 71, 72), and a notice of appearance (Dkt. 68), all filed August 7. Yesterday's briefing flagged these filings and noted the identities of the admitting attorneys and their clients as unverified from the ground truth alone. That remains true today: no primary-source motion papers have been surfaced to confirm who entered the case. The pattern itself — a paired cluster of pro hac vice admissions arriving on a Friday, roughly three weeks into an active Chapter 11 — warrants continued attention, but absent confirmed identities it carries no actionable implication for the recovery posture.

No new press coverage dated August 8 has emerged. The most recent secondary reporting remains the August 5 Herald-Dispatch and Charleston Gazette-Mail articles already covered. Those pieces added regional texture to the governance fight — specifically, 
Gassheimer's account that TRAG/RGE filed counterclaims and a TRO motion in the West Virginia action on July 21 seeking to restore Nathan as Independent Manager, and that the West Virginia court denied that TRO on July 24
 — and they confirm that the Hindman management team has characterized 
the $75.6 million Dynamic Finance check as "uncertified," rejected for lack of transparency regarding the source of funds
. Neither development is new to the Delaware docket; they are factual anchors for the governance contest whose resolution, or escalation, will shape the August 19 objection period. One additional data point from regional coverage that has not been fully absorbed: 
prior management entered into a power purchase agreement in December 2025 with Element H, an affiliate owned by the Hodson family, at prices alleged to be below the cost of generation, with potential losses cited at $1 billion
 — __[News and Sentinel](https://www.newsandsentinel.com/news/business/2026/08/power-struggle-new-pleasants-power-leadership-fights-with-former-management-in-bankruptcy-filings/)__. That allegation is unverified (it appears in Hindman's declaration, not in a court ruling), but if substantiated it would materially widen the universe of potential estate claims and, by extension, the recovery pool available to unsecured creditors including the WVEDA.

Today's concrete task is a factual one: confirm from the underlying motion papers the identities of the counsel and parties behind Dkt. 69–72. Until those are known, the significance of Friday's appearance cluster — whether it represents a significant creditor, an adverse party organizing into the governance dispute, or a potential § 363 bidder — cannot be assessed. The next hard milestone is August 19, 2026, the objection deadline for the first-day operational orders set by Dkt. 57, followed by the September 3 final hearing before Judge Karen Owens in Courtroom 3, 824 Market Street, Wilmington, at 1:00 PM.

items.body_md:
The press coverage that landed August 5–6 fills in the structural detail on Anthropic's Concord II partial dismissal motions that yesterday's edition flagged at the level of their existence and general thrust. The more precise picture, now confirmed across multiple sources, is that Anthropic is not seeking to dismiss the core torrenting and training allegations — those remain live — but is instead targeting two specific, downstream claims: the output-based infringement count, and a Digital Millennium Copyright Act count. 
Anthropic argued that the complaint, covering roughly 21,000 works, never cites one instance of Claude reproducing a lyric, and asked that the output claim be dismissed with prejudice.
 The "with prejudice" ask is the sharpest edge here: if granted, the publishers would be barred from replying that claim in its current form, eliminating what would otherwise be the most direct mechanism to show consumer-facing harm at trial. 
Anthropic also moved to dismiss the DMCA count, arguing the statute reaches only the stripping of copyright management information from a complete work, and that the publishers never allege Anthropic held their full compositions.
 That DMCA theory, if it had survived, would have provided a separate damages floor independent of statutory copyright damages — its loss narrows the publishers' damages architecture in Concord II, though it has no direct bearing on the infringement claims already advancing in 5:24-cv-03811. 
The two filings landed on Monday, August 3, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.



Concord II carries case number 5:26-cv-00880, was filed January 28, 2026, and names Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as individual defendants
 — the confirmed case number is worth logging cleanly given the parallel docket management now running alongside 5:24-cv-03811. 
Amodei filed separately to get the direct infringement count against him personally dropped; Anthropic did not move against the torrenting and training claims, which it continues to contest.
 The strategic implication for rights-holders in both proceedings is that Anthropic has chosen to fight the input-side allegations on the merits while attempting to clear the output-side and DMCA theories at the pleading stage — a posture that, if successful, would concentrate the entire evidentiary burden of the litigation on the training-data conduct and away from anything Claude does in response to user prompts. Whether the publishers can amend to supply the missing output examples, or whether the court grants dismissal with prejudice on that count, will materially affect the damages ceiling they can present to any jury in Concord II.

Nothing new has landed on the Concord I docket (5:24-cv-03811) since yesterday's edition. The next concrete event remains the Case Management Conference before Judge Lee on Zoom on September 2, 2026, followed by the Summary Judgment Hearing on October 21, 2026 — at which the fair use and direct infringement questions in the original case will be the focus. The Concord II partial dismissal argument on November 4 then follows, meaning Judge Lee will have issued her summary judgment ruling in Concord I, or will be close to doing so, at the point she hears the threshold pleading challenges in Concord II. That sequencing matters: a summary judgment ruling adverse to Anthropic on training-data fair use in Concord I would substantially undercut the legal premise of the same argument Anthropic is mounting in Concord II.

*In re Terraform Labs Pte. Ltd., Bankr. D. Del., Case No. 24-10070-BLS, Judge Brendan Linehan Shannon*

The only new docket activity since Wednesday's edition is Dkt. 1319, an Objection filed August 5, 2026. The docket entry designation — "Objection" without further qualification in the publicly available record — places it squarely in the pattern that has defined this estate's post-confirmation phase: contested claim allowance, disputed claim transfers, or resistance to a pending motion. The filing lands two days after a cluster of four claim transfers (Dkts. 1309–1312, August 3), the most recent of which assigned a $3,454,036.42 claim from a redacted transferor to Serrur Investment Partners, LP via TerraClaim LLC, signaling continued secondary-market activity in the claims pool. Whether Dkt. 1319 targets one of those transfers, challenges a valuation determination on the crypto loss claims register, or contests some other pending matter cannot be confirmed from publicly available sources as of this briefing; the filing's substance requires PACER access to the full document.

What is clear is the structural context: 
more than two years after Terraform Labs entered chapter 11, its confirmed liquidating plan remains in active administration, and as of the post-confirmation report for the quarter ending March 31, 2026, the Wind Down Trust had distributed nothing to plan creditors, even as the plan administrator continued reconciling more than 16,000 crypto loss claims and pressing a $4 billion lawsuit against Jump Trading as the estate's largest affirmative recovery effort
 (__[Elevenflo](https://elevenflo.com/blog/terraform-labs-bankruptcy)__). An objection at Dkt. 1319 — whatever its precise target — lands in an estate where claim allowance determinations are the direct gating mechanism for eventual distributions. Any successful objection that disallows or reduces a claim expands the recoverable pool for remaining allowed creditors; any objection that fails preserves a competing draw on that pool. The post-confirmation reports filed July 30 (Dkts. 1306–1307) will also repay review once accessible, as they will reflect the trust's asset position for the most recent quarterly period and may reveal whether the cash runway supports the litigation posture in the Jump and Jane Street proceedings.

The next concrete milestone to track is any response deadline or hearing date tied to Dkt. 1319, which under Local Rule 9006-1(c) would typically run 14 days from service absent a separate scheduling order. On the litigation front, the plan administrator's motion to dismiss the Chang adversary proceeding (Adv. Proc. 26-50229) remains pending before Judge Shannon following the July 2026 filing reported last month (__[Law360](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy-authority/mid-cap/articles/2504885)__), and the Jane Street insider-trading action in the Southern District of New York continues to be contested on the motion-to-dismiss briefing that closed in June (__[Law360](https://www.law360.com/bankruptcy/articles/2489043)__). Neither of those proceedings generated new docket activity in the lookback window.
